content.title: LCOE Modelling: Comparing Costs, Guiding Decisions

content.text:
By the end of this lesson, you will have learned how the DREI framework uses levelized cost of electricity 💬️ (LCOE) modelling to connect investment risk, financing costs, and renewable energy competitiveness. You will understand how public instruments affect the weighted average cost of capital (WACC), and how these changes translate into lower LCOE values for renewable projects.
The lesson does not focus on detailed financial modelling techniques, which have already been introduced earlier in the Academy. Instead, it emphasizes the role of LCOE within the DREI framework: providing a consistent, transparent metric to compare the impact of different derisking strategies across technologies and country contexts.
By working through this lesson, you will see how policymakers and stakeholders can use LCOE results to evaluate trade-offs, prioritize public interventions, and communicate the benefits of derisking in clear, quantifiable terms.

content.title: A: Calculating Life Cycle Costs and incremental costs of renewable energy investment

content.text:
The modelling of the Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) helps to evaluate the cost competitiveness of the renewable energy technology under consideration. LCOE represents the average cost of electricity generation over the lifetime of a project, incorporating investment, operation, maintenance, and financing costs. It provides a clear, comparable metric for assessing the economic viability of different energy technologies.

The LCOE is calculated using the DREI LCOE Tool, which combines technical and financial inputs based on the national and technological context. These include data on capital expenditure, operations and maintenance, system lifetime, generation performance, and financing conditions. The tool uses the financing costs identified earlier in the process—both before and after the application of public derisking instruments.

Data collection for this modelling involves technical assumptions that can often be drawn from national energy planning or feasibility studies. Financial parameters, particularly the cost of equity and debt, are based on investor input collected through structured interviews. In some contexts, barriers to obtaining accurate data may include lack of transparency, limited availability of disaggregated cost figures, or uncertain pricing of fossil fuel alternatives.

metadata.title: LCOE for the marginal baseline and wind investment in Kenya
metadata.subtitle: In the 2013 case study on utility-scale wind, the LCOE was calculated based on a representative wind project in Kenya. The modelling used technical performance data and financing assumptions reflecting the country’s investment environment at the time. The LCOE under current risk conditions was then compared with a revised value that accounted for the expected improvements in financing terms resulting from public measures such as credit guarantees and permitting reforms. This post-derisking LCOE was also compared to the cost of electricity from fossil fuel-based generation, providing a benchmark for understanding the potential economic benefit of supporting wind energy development.
metadata.footnote: Source: United Nations Development Programme, 2013. Derisking Renewable Energy Investment: A Framework to Support Policymakers in Selecting Public Instruments to Promote Renewable Energy Investment in Developing Countries. New York: United Nations Development Programme.

metadata.title: Kenya: LCOE for diesel and solar mini-grids
metadata.subtitle: In the 2018 study on solar mini-grids in Kenya, the LCOE modelling examined the electricity cost of solar PV-battery systems in rural areas. Diesel generation was used as the baseline technology. The initial LCOE reflected the high financing costs faced by mini-grid developers. After modelling the impact of selected derisking instruments—such as concessional loans, standardised regulation, and output-based subsidies—the post-derisking LCOE showed a clear reduction. The comparison with the baseline highlighted that mini-grids, when supported by targeted public instruments, could offer a competitive and sustainable alternative for rural electrification.
metadata.footnote: Source: UNDP & ETH Zurich (2018). Derisking Renewable Energy Investment: Off-Grid Electrification. United Nations Development Programme, New York, NY and ETH Zurich, Energy Politics Group, Zurich, Switzerland.

takeaways.title: LCOE Modelling Lets You Compare Renewable and Fossil Costs
takeaways.description: The LCOE modelling provides estimates of the Business as Usual electricity production costs (LCOE) for the Baseline technology (usually a fossil fuel based technology) and for the renewable energy technology considered in the study

takeaways.title: Derisking Shows How Renewables Can Compete with Business-as-Usual
takeaways.description: The impacts of the derisking instruments on the cost of capital are evaluated, and the resulting LCOE for the renewable energy technology after derisking is compared with the Business-as-Usual LCOEs.
